content: PRR32, also known as CXorf64 (Chromosome X Open Reading Frame 64), is a protein encoded by the CXorf64 gene in humans. Homologs of the PRR32 gene are conserved across several species, including chimpanzees, rhesus monkeys, dogs, cows, mice, and rats. According to NCBI data, orthologs of the human PRR32 gene are present in 82 different organisms. The PRR32 gene appears to be associated with a group of genes that are overexpressed in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), as demonstrated in a study analyzing gene expression patterns in muscle tissues from patients with ALS and multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN). Gene Characteristics The CXorf64 gene is located on the X chromosome at position Xq25 and spans 2023 base pairs, which is relatively small compared to other genes. It is situated on the antisense (+) strand. The gene is flanked upstream by DKAF12L1 and downstream by LOC10, with CXorf64 represented as the central blue column in genomic diagrams. Transcript Information CXorf64 contains a single exon, which produces one transcript variant. This gene is predominantly expressed in muscle tissue, and no alternative isoforms of CXorf64 have been identified. Protein Properties Structure The predicted tertiary structure of the PRR32 protein is characterized by long alpha-helices located at the terminal regions opposite the Nand C-terminal ends. Expression Microarray-based tissue expression analysis from NCBI GEO indicates that CXorf64 has average expression levels in most tissues. However, it exhibits relatively low expression in the prostate, heart, fat, and endometrium (approximately the 25th percentile of tissue gene expression). Most microarray studies have reported very low levels of gene expression across all assessed tissues. The Human Protein Atlas suggests higher expression of the gene in the heart, prostate, and fat tissues, although no tissue-specific data were available from the Allen Brain Atlas or GenePaint. Subcellular Localization The PRR32 protein is synthesized in the cytoplasm and is predicted to localize to the mitochondria. Additional predicted localizations include the nucleus, plasma membrane, extracellular space, peroxisome, and cytosol. Post-Translational Modifications PRR32 undergoes several post-translational modifications, including N-linked glycosylation at multiple predicted sites with high confidence. Glycosylation plays a role in cell-cell adhesion, particularly through sugar-binding proteins involved in immune system mechanisms. A graph illustrates the predicted N-glycosylation sites along the protein chain, with specific regions identified as glycosylated. Homology and Evolution Orthologs of PRR32 were identified using NCBI BLAST and UCSC BLAT tools. These analyses generated a list of orthologs across more than 80 species, which was narrowed down to 30 species for further study. Among primates, which are genetically closest to humans, the similarity to the human PRR32 gene ranged from 95% to 99%. Excluding primates, the analysis identified orthologs in mammals such as rabbits, dogs, ferrets, and rhinos, with similarity percentages between 69% and 89%. When all mammals were excluded, no matches were found, indicating that the PRR32 gene is relevant only in mammals. The protein sequences of PRR32 are highly conserved among closely related species, such as chimpanzees, gorillas, and orangutans. Clinical Significance Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) A study analyzed gene expression patterns in muscle tissues from ALS and MMN patients compared to controls using a 0ST array. Over 3000 genes were identified with significant expression differences (q < 10%). Among 50 genes overexpressed exclusively in ALS patients were leucine-rich repeat kinase-2, follistatin, collagen type XIX alpha-1, ceramide kinase-like, sestrin-3, and CXorf64. No genes were significantly overexpressed in MMN alone. Genes underexpressed only in ALS included actinin alpha-3, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase-2, and homeobox C10, while underexpressed genes in MMN included hemoglobin A1 and CXorf64. Ankyrin repeat domain-1 was overexpressed in both ALS and MMN groups. Genes underexpressed in both groups included myosin light chain kinase-2, enolase-3, and 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase-1. Validation using RT-PCR confirmed the differential expression of leucine-rich repeat kinase-2, follistatin, collagen type XIX alpha-1, ceramide kinase-like, sestrin-3, and CXorf64. In conclusion, there is differential tissue-specific gene expression in ALS patients compared to MMN patients and controls. Further studies are required to evaluate these identified genes in larger patient cohorts and across different tissues.
